exampleAnswers.title: Determining the Continuity of a Vector Function

question.text: Determine the interval on which the function $\mathbf f(t) = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{t^2-1} \\ \sqrt{t} \\ t+3 \end{bmatrix}$ is continuous.
question.explanation:
A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's now consider the components of $\mathbf f (t)$ one by one.

  • The function $\dfrac{1}{t^2-1}$ is continuous everywhere except the excluded points $t=\pm{1}.$

  • The function $\sqrt{t}$ is continuous for $t\geq 0.$

  • The function $t+3$ is continuous for all real numbers.

Therefore, the vector-valued function $\mathbf f (t)$ is continuous for all $t\geq 0$ except the point $t=1.$ So the interval of continuity is $[0,1) \cup (1,\infty).$

question.text: Determine the interval on which the function $\mathbf f (t) = \dfrac {t^2+4t}t\, \mathbf i + (t^2-1) \,\mathbf j + \dfrac1 {t-2}\,\mathbf k $ is continuous.
question.explanation:
A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's now consider the components of $\mathbf f (t)$ one-by-one.

  • The function $\dfrac {t^2+4t}t$ is continuous everywhere except the excluded point $t=0.$

  • The function $t^2-1$ is continuous for all real numbers.

  • The function $\dfrac1 {t-2}$ is continuous everywhere except the point $t=2.$

Therefore, the vector-valued function $\mathbf f (t)$ is continuous everywhere except the points $t=0$ and $t=2.$ So the interval of continuity is $(-\infty, 0)\cup\left(0, 2\right)\cup\left(2, \infty\right).$

example.title: Determining the Continuity of a Vector Function

question.text:
Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous on $[-1, 1]?$

\begin{align*} \mathbf p (s) &=|s^2-1| \, \mathbf i + \dfrac {s+1} {s} \,\mathbf j + 2 s^2 \,\mathbf k\\[3pt] \mathbf q (s) &= \ln(s-1)\, \mathbf i + (s^2+1) \,\mathbf j + \cos{s}\,\mathbf k\\[3pt] \mathbf r (s) &= \sin{s}\, \mathbf i - 2\tan{s} \,\mathbf j + \csc{s}\,\mathbf k \end{align*}
question.choice1: None of the functions are continuous on $[-1,1]$
question.explanation:
A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's consider the functions one by one.

  • The function $\mathbf p(s)$ is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$ because its second component, $\dfrac {s+1} {s},$ is undefined at $s = 0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1, 1].$

  • The function $\mathbf q(s)$ is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$ because its first component, $\ln(s - 1)$, is undefined at $s = 1$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1, 1].$

  • The function $\mathbf r(s)$ is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$ because its third component, $\csc{s}$, is undefined at $s = 0$ and hence discontinuous on $[-1, 1].$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the functions are continuous on $[-1, 1].$"

example.title: Determining the Continuity of a Vector Function

question.text: Which of the following vector-valued functions are continuous at $t=0?$ \begin{align*} \mathbf f (t) &= \cot t\, \mathbf i + 3t^3 \,\mathbf j + (2t+1)\,\mathbf k \\[3pt] \mathbf g (t) &= \dfrac 2 t\, \mathbf i + t^3 \,\mathbf j + \sin t\,\mathbf k \\[3pt] \mathbf h (t) &= 2t\, \mathbf i + \cos t \,\mathbf j + t^4\,\mathbf k \end{align*}
question.choice5: All the functions are continuous at $t=0$
question.explanation:
A vector-valued function is continuous at a point if and only if each of its components is continuous at that point.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

  • Function $\mathbf f (t)$ is not continuous at $t=0$ since its first component $\cot t$ is not continuous at $t=0.$ Indeed, the left and right limits are not equal: \begin{align*} \lim_{t \to +0} \cot t = +\infty \\[3pt] \lim_{t \to -0}\cot t = -\infty \end{align*} Hence, $\lim\limits_{t \to 0} \cot t $ doesn’t exist.

  • Function $\mathbf g (t)$ is not continuous at $t=0$ since its first component $\dfrac 2 t$ is not continuous at $t=0.$

  • Function $\mathbf h (t)$ is continuous at $t=0$ because each of its components $2t$, $\cos t$ and $t^4$ are continuous at $t=0.$

Therefore, the answer is:

$\qquad$ $\mathbf h (t)$ only.

example.title: Determining the Continuity of a Vector Function

question.text: Determine the interval on which the function $\mathbf f (t) = \left \langle t\cos{2t}, \, 2e^{\large{t-1}}, \, \sqrt{5-t} \right \rangle$ is continuous.
question.explanation:
A vector-valued function is continuous on an interval if and only if each of its components is continuous on that interval.

Let's now consider the components of $\mathbf f (t)$ one by one.

  • The function $t\cos{2t}$ is continuous for all real numbers.

  • The function $2e^{\large{t-1}}$ is continuous for all real numbers.

  • The function $\sqrt{5-t}$ is continuous for $t \leq 5.$

Therefore, the vector-valued function $\mathbf f (t)$ is continuous for $t \leq 5.$ So the interval of continuity is $(-\infty, 5 ].$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Value of a Vector Function Using Properties of Continuous Functions

question.text: Find $\mathbf f(5)$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are two continuous vector-valued functions for which $\mathbf g(5)=\left\langle -1 , 1 , -2 \right\rangle$ and \[\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5} \left[\mathbf f(t)+ 3\mathbf g(t)\right]=\left\langle 1 , 3 , 1\right\rangle\!.\]
question.explanation:
Using the addition rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get
\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5} \left[\mathbf f(t)+3\mathbf g(t)\right] &=\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5} \mathbf f(t)+ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5}[3\mathbf g(t)]\\[5pt] &= \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5} \mathbf f(t)+3\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5}\mathbf g(t)\\[5pt] &=\mathbf f(5)+ 3\mathbf g(5)\\[5pt] &=\mathbf f(5)+ 3 \underbrace{\left\langle -1 , 1 , -2 \right\rangle}_{\mathbf g(5)} \\[5pt] &= \mathbf f(5)+ \left\langle -3 , 3 , -6 \right\rangle. \end{align*}

On the other hand, we are told that \[ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5} \left[\mathbf f(t)+ 3\mathbf g(t)\right]=\left\langle 1 ,3 , 1\right\rangle. \]

Therefore, we obtain the following equation which we can solve for $\mathbf{f} (5)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 5} \left[\mathbf f(t)+3\mathbf g(t)\right] &= \left\langle 1 , 3 , 1\right\rangle \\[5pt] \mathbf f(5) + \left\langle -3 , 3 , -6\right\rangle&=\left\langle 1 , 3, 1 \right\rangle \\[5pt] \mathbf f(5) &=\left\langle 1 , 3, 1 \right\rangle - \left\langle -3 , 3 , -6\right\rangle \\[5pt] \mathbf f(5) &= \left\langle 4 , 0 , 7\right\rangle \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Value of a Vector Function Using Properties of Continuous Functions

question.text: Given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are two continuous vector-valued functions for which $\mathbf f(-7) = \left\langle 6, 0, -2 \right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(-7) = \left\langle 2, -1, 0 \right\rangle,$ determine \[\lim_\limits{t\to -7}\left[\dfrac{\mathbf f(t)}{2}+3\mathbf g(t)\right].\]
question.explanation:
Using the constant multiple and the addition rule for limits, we get

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\to -7} \left[\dfrac{\mathbf f(t)}{2}+3\mathbf g(t)\right] &=\lim_\limits{t\to -7}\dfrac{\mathbf f(t)}{2}+\lim_\limits{t\to -7}3\mathbf g(t)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\lim_\limits{t\to -7} \mathbf f(t)+3\lim_\limits{t\to -7}\mathbf g(t) . \end{align*}

Now, using the fact that both functions are continuous, we get:

\begin{align*} \dfrac 1 2\lim_\limits{t\to -7} \mathbf f(t)+3\lim_\limits{t\to -7}\mathbf g(t) &= \dfrac 1 2 \mathbf f(-7)+3\mathbf g(-7)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left\langle 6 , 0, -2 \right\rangle + 3\left\langle 2, -1, 0 \right\rangle\\[5pt] &= \left\langle 3 , 0, -1 \right\rangle + \left\langle 6, -3, 0 \right\rangle\\[5pt] &= \left\langle 9 , -3, -1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Value of a Vector Function Using Properties of Continuous Functions

question.text: Find $\mathbf f(0)$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ is a continuous vector-valued function and $u(t)$ is continuous real-valued function for which $u(0) =3 $ and \[ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \big[ u(t) \mathbf f(t) \big] = \left\langle -18, -21, 6 \right\rangle\!. \]
question.explanation:
Using the scalar function multiple rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \left[u(t) \mathbf f(t) \right] &= \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} u(t) \cdot\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0}\mathbf f(t)\\[3pt] &= u(0) \mathbf f(0)\\[3pt] &= 3\mathbf f(0) \end{align*}

On the other hand, we are told that \[ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \big[ u(t) \mathbf f(t) \big] = \left\langle-18, -21, 6 \right\rangle\!. \]

Therefore, we obtain the following equation which we can solve for $\mathbf{f} (0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \left[ u(t) \mathbf f(t) \right]&=\left\langle -18, -21, 6\right\rangle \\[3pt] 3\mathbf f(0) &= \left\langle -18, -21, 6 \right\rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf f(0) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \left\langle -18, -21, 6\right\rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf f(0) &= \left\langle -6 , -7 , 2\right\rangle \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Value of a Vector Function Using Properties of Continuous Functions

question.text: Find $\mathbf g(2)$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are two continuous vector-valued functions for which $\mathbf f(2) = \left\langle 1, 1, 2 \right\rangle$ and \[ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2} \big[ \mathbf f(t)+2\mathbf g(t) \big] = \left\langle -1, 7, 0 \right\rangle\!. \]
question.explanation:
Using the constant multiple, and the addition rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2} \left[\mathbf f(t)+2\mathbf g(t)\right] &= \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2} \mathbf f(t)+\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2}2\mathbf g(t)\\[3pt] &= \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2} \mathbf f(t)+2\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2}\mathbf g(t)\\[3pt] &= \mathbf f(2)+2\mathbf g(2)\\[3pt] &= \underbrace{\left\langle 1 , 1, 2 \right\rangle}_{\large \mathbf f(2)} + 2\mathbf g(2) \end{align*}

On the other hand, we are told that \[ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2} \left[\mathbf f(t)+2\mathbf g(t)\right] =\left\langle -1 , 7 , 0\right\rangle \]

Therefore, we obtain the following equation which we can solve for $\mathbf{g} (2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 2} \left[\mathbf f(t)+2\mathbf g(t)\right]&=\left\langle -1 , 7 , 0\right\rangle \\[3pt] \left\langle 1 , 1, 2 \right\rangle+2\mathbf g(2) &= \left\langle -1 , 7 , 0\right\rangle \\[3pt] 2\mathbf g(2) &= \left\langle -1 , 7 , 0\right\rangle - \left\langle 1 , 1, 2 \right\rangle \\[3pt] 2\mathbf g(2) &= \left\langle -2 , 6 , -2\right\rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf g(2) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \left\langle -2 , 6 , -2\right\rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf g(2) &= \left\langle -1 , 3 , -1\right\rangle \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Value of a Vector Function Using Properties of Continuous Functions

question.text: Find $\mathbf f(0)$ given that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are two continuous vector-valued functions for which $\mathbf g(0)=\left\langle -1 , 0 , 1 \right\rangle$ and \[\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \left[\mathbf f(t)-\mathbf g(t)\right]=\left\langle -2 , -3 , 0\right\rangle\!.\]
question.choice5: The value of $\mathbf f(0)$ cannot be determined.
question.explanation:
Using the addition rule for limits, and the fact that both functions are continuous, we get:

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \left[\mathbf f(t)-\mathbf g(t)\right] &=\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \mathbf f(t)+ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0}[-\mathbf g(t)]\\[3pt] &= \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \mathbf f(t)-\lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0}\mathbf g(t)\\[3pt] &=\mathbf f(0)- \mathbf g(0)\\[3pt] &=\mathbf f(0)- \underbrace{\left\langle -1 , 0 , 1 \right\rangle}_{\mathbf g(0)} \end{align*}

On the other hand, we are told that: \[ \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \left[\mathbf f(t)-\mathbf g(t)\right]=\left\langle -2 , -3 , 0\right\rangle \]

Therefore, we obtain the following equation which we can solve for $\mathbf{f} (0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \lim_\limits{t\rightarrow 0} \left[\mathbf f(t)-\mathbf g(t)\right] &= \left\langle -2 , -3 , 0\right\rangle \\[3pt] \left\langle -2 , -3 , 0\right\rangle&=\mathbf f(0)-\left\langle -1 , 0, 1 \right\rangle \\[3pt] \left\langle -2 , -3 , 0\right\rangle+\left\langle -1 , 0, 1 \right\rangle&=\mathbf f(0) \\[3pt] \mathbf f(0) &= \left\langle -3 , -3 , 1\right\rangle \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Determining the Differentiability of a Vector Function

question.text: Determine the interval on which the function $\mathbf f (t) =\sqrt{t}\, \mathbf i + \dfrac{1}{t-4} \,\mathbf j -5 t^2\,\mathbf k $ is differentiable.
question.explanation:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf f (t)$ is defined on the interval $[0,4)\cup(4,\infty).$ Let's study the differentiability of its components on this interval one-by-one.

  • The derivative of $\sqrt{t}$ is \[ \left(\sqrt{t}\right)'=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{t}} . \] Since the derivative is not defined at $t=0,$ we conclude that $\sqrt{t}$ is not differentiable at this point.

  • The derivative of $\dfrac{1}{t-4}$ is \[ \left(\dfrac{1}{t-4}\right)'=-\dfrac{1}{(t-4)^2} . \] Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $[0,4)\cup(4,\infty),$ we conclude that $\dfrac{1}{t-4}$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • The derivative of $-5 t^2$ is \[ \left(-5 t^2\right)'=-10t . \] Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $[0,4)\cup(4,\infty),$ we conclude that $-5 t^2$ is differentiable on this interval.

Taking into account that all the components of $\mathbf f (t)$ are differentiable for all the points on the interval $[0,4)\cup(4,\infty),$ except the point $t=0,$ we conclude that $\mathbf f (t)$ is differentiable on $(0,4)\cup(4,\infty).$

topic.name: Continuity and Differentiability of Vector-Valued Functions

example.title: Determining the Differentiability of a Vector Function

question.text: Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t \in (\pi, 2\pi)?$ \begin{align*} \mathbf f (t) &= \left \langle \sin^2 t, \: \dfrac 1 t, \: \sin t - \cos t \right \rangle\\[5pt] \mathbf g (t) &=\left \langle t\sqrt t, \: 1-t^2, \: t\sin(2t) \right \rangle\\[5pt] \mathbf h (t) & = \left \langle \cos(2t), \: 2t, \: \cos t \right \rangle\\ \end{align*}
question.choice1: All the functions are differentiable on $ (\pi, 2\pi)$
question.choice5: None of the functions are differentiable on $(\pi, 2\pi)$
question.explanation:
All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all $t\in (\pi, 2\pi).$

A function is differentiable on the interval $(\pi, 2\pi)$ if and only if each of its component functions is differentiable on that interval.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

  • We differentiate $\mathbf f(t)$ to find $\mathbf f'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \mathbf f'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\sin^2t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left(\dfrac 1 t \right), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\sin t-\cos t) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 2\sin t \cos t, \: -\dfrac 1 {t^2}, \: \cos t + \sin t\rangle \end{align} Since each component of $\mathbf f '(t)$ is defined for all $t \in (\pi, 2\pi)$, we conclude that $\mathbf f(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • Next, we differentiate $\mathbf g(t)$ to find $\mathbf g'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \mathbf g'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t\sqrt t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (1-t^2), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t \sin(2t)) \right \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t^{3/2}), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (1-t^2), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t \sin(2t)) \right \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left \langle \dfrac 3 2 t^{1/2}, \: -2t, \: \sin(2t) + 2t\cos(2t) \right \rangle \\[5pt] &= \left \langle \dfrac 3 2\sqrt t, \: -2t, \: \sin(2t) + 2t\cos(2t) \right \rangle \end{align} Since each component of $\mathbf g' (t)$ is defined for all $t\in (\pi, 2\pi)$, we have that $\mathbf g(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • Finally, we differentiate $\mathbf h(t)$ to find $\mathbf h'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \mathbf h'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \cos(2t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (2t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\cos t ) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle -2\sin(2t), \: 2, \: -\sin t \right \rangle \end{align} Since each component of $\mathbf h' (t)$ is defined for all $t \in (\pi, 2\pi)$, we conclude that $\mathbf h(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is:

$\qquad$ All the functions are differentiable on $ (\pi, 2\pi).$

example.title: Determining the Differentiability of a Vector Function

question.text: Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in[0,1]?$ \begin{align*} \mathbf p (t) &= \left \langle t - 1, \: e^t, \: t^3 \right \rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf q (t) &= \left \langle 1, \: \sin(2t), \: \sqrt[3]{2t-1} \right \rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf r (t) &= \left \langle 3t + 2, \: |t|, \: \cos^2{t} \right \rangle \end{align*}
question.choice5: None of the functions are differentiable on $t\in[0,1]$
question.explanation:
All of these vector-valued functions are defined for all $t \in [0,1].$

A function is differentiable on the interval $t\in[0, 1]$ if and only if each component is differentiable on that interval.

Let's now consider the functions one by one.

  • We differentiate $\mathbf p(t)$ to find $\mathbf p'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf p'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t-1), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (e^t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t^3) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 1, \: e^t, \: 3t^2 \rangle \end{align*} Since each component of $\mathbf p '(t)$ is defined on $[0, 1],$ we conclude that $\mathbf p(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • Next, we differentiate $\mathbf q(t)$ to find $\mathbf q'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf q'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (1), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\sin{t}), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left( \sqrt[3]{2t-1} \right) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle 0, \: 2\cos{t} , \: \dfrac{2}{3 \sqrt[3]{(2 t - 1)^2}} \right \rangle \end{align*} Since the third component of this vector, $\dfrac{2}{3 \sqrt[3]{(2 t - 1)^2}}, $ is undefined at $t=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we conclude that the function $\mathbf q(t)$ is not differentiable on $[0, 1].$

  • Finally, since the deviative of the second component $|t|$ of $\mathbf r(t)$ is undefined at $t=0,$ we conclude that $\mathbf r(t)$ is not differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is "$\mathbf p (t) $ only."

example.title: Determining the Differentiability of a Vector Function

question.text: Determine the interval on which the function $\mathbf f (t) =\sin{3t}\, \mathbf i + \sqrt{t^2-1} \,\mathbf j -\cos{t}\,\mathbf k $ is differentiable.
question.explanation:
The vector-valued function $\mathbf f (t)$ is defined on the interval $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty).$ Let's study the differentiability of its components on this interval one by one.

  • The derivative of $\sin{3t}$ is \[ \left(\sin{3t}\right)'=3\cos{t} . \] Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty),$ we conclude that $\sin{3t}$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • The derivative of $\sqrt{t^2-1}$ is \[ \left(\sqrt{t^2-1}\right)'=\dfrac{t}{\sqrt{t^2 - 1}}. \] Since the derivative is not defined at $t = \pm 1,$ we conclude that $\sqrt{t^2-1}$ is not differentiable at this points.

  • The derivative of $-\cos{t}$ is \[ \left(-\cos{t}\right)'=\sin{t} . \] Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty),$ we conclude that $-\cos{t}$ is differentiable on this interval.

Taking into account that all the components of $\mathbf f (t)$ are differentiable for all the points on the interval $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty),$ except the points $t=\pm 1,$ we conclude that $\mathbf f (t)$ is differentiable on $(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty).$

topic.name: Continuity and Differentiability of Vector-Valued Functions

example.title: Determining the Differentiability of a Vector Function

question.text: Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in(0,1)?$ \begin{align*} \mathbf p (t) &= \left \langle 2t - 1, \: t^2 + 4, \: -e^t \right \rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf q (t) &= \left \langle (t+1)^4, \: \sqrt[3] t, \: \ln t \right \rangle \\[3pt] \mathbf r (t) &= \left \langle 3t + 2, \: \arctan t, \: t^2 - 2 \right \rangle \end{align*}
question.choice1: All the functions are differentiable on $t\in(0,1)$
question.choice5: None of the functions are differentiable on $t\in(0,1)$
question.explanation:
All of these vector-valued functions are defined on $t\in(0, 1).$

A function is differentiable on the interval $t\in(0, 1)$ if and only if each component is differentiable on that interval.

Let's now consider the functions one-by-one.

  • We differentiate $\mathbf p(t)$ to find $\mathbf p'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf p'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (2t-1), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t^2 + 4), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (-e^t) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 2, \: 2t, \: -e^{t} \rangle \end{align*} Since each component of $\mathbf p '(t)$ is defined on $t\in(0, 1)$, we conclude that $\mathbf p(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • Next, we differentiate $\mathbf q(t)$ to find $\mathbf q'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf q'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} ((t+1)^4), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\sqrt[3] t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\ln t) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle 4(t+1)^3, \: \dfrac 1 {3 \sqrt[3] {t^2}}, \: \dfrac 1 t \right \rangle \end{align*} Since each component of $\mathbf q' (t)$ is defined on $t\in(0, 1)$, we have that $\mathbf q(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

  • Finally, we differentiate $\mathbf r(t)$ to find $\mathbf r'(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= \left \langle \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left(3t + 2\right), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (\arctan t), \: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (t^2 - 2 ) \right \rangle \\[3pt] &=\left \langle 3, \: \dfrac{1}{1+ t^2}, \: 2t \right \rangle \end{align*} Since each component of $\mathbf r' (t)$ is defined on $t\in(0, 1)$, we conclude that $\mathbf r(t)$ is differentiable on this interval.

Therefore, the answer is:

$\qquad$ All the functions are differentiable on $(0,1).$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Interval on Which a Product of Functions is Differentiable

question.text: Find the interval where the function $\mathbf f(t)=u(t)\mathbf g(t)$ is differentiable, given that \begin{align*} u(t)&=t^2+2\\[3pt] \mathbf g(t) &=\sqrt[3]{t-3}\,\mathbf i+\cos^2{t}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{1+t^2}\,\mathbf k \end{align*}
question.explanation:
The function $\mathbf f(t)=u(t)\mathbf g(t)$ is differentiable on the common domain where both $u(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are differentiable. The vector function $\mathbf g(t)$ is differentiable on the common domain where its components are differentiable.

Let's now find the intervals where each of the functions $u(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are differentiable.

For the real-valued function $u(t)\mathbin{:}$

  • We observe that $u(t)$ is differentiable for all values of $t \in (-\infty, \infty).$

For the function $\mathbf g(t)\mathbin{:}$
